title: Cross-Site Scripting
brief: **Ticket:** a greeting page reflects your name straight into the HTML. A simulated admin bot visits pages. Land a script and steal what the bot leaks.
theory:
## What it is
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is getting your JavaScript to run in another user's
browser, in the context of a trusted site. The app reflects or stores your input
into a page without encoding it.

## How it works
Send `name=<script>alert(1)</script>`; if the server drops it straight into the
HTML, the victim's browser executes it. **Reflected** XSS bounces off a single
request (a crafted link). **Stored** XSS is saved (a comment, a profile) and
fires for everyone who views it. Payloads steal session cookies, perform actions
as the victim, or rewrite the page.

## In the real world
The 2005 **Samy worm** used stored XSS to add over a million MySpace friends in a
day. The 2014 **TweetDeck** XSS made tweets auto-retweet themselves across the
platform. XSS remains one of the most reported bug-bounty classes.

## How to prevent it
**Context-aware output encoding** - HTML-encode data when writing it into HTML so
`<script>` becomes harmless text. Add a **Content-Security-Policy** header as a
strong second layer, and set cookies `HttpOnly` so script cannot read them.
worked_example:
``` $ curl "https://x/greet?name="

Hello

# runs in the victim's browser ```

investigation.intro: Reflect a script payload off a live app, then watch output encoding neutralise it.
steps:
**Start the lab app** (leave it running; open a *second* terminal tab for the attack):
```bash
cd /workspaces/examto/appsec-lab
python3 -m venv .venv 2>/dev/null; . .venv/bin/activate; pip install -q -r requirements.txt
python3 run_server.py
```

In a second terminal, send a script payload into the greeting and look at the raw HTML that comes back - your `<script>` is embedded verbatim:
```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5000/greet?name=<script>alert(1)</script>"
```
In a real browser that script would execute as the victim.

**Apply the fix and re-test.** Stop the server (Ctrl+C) and restart it in secure mode, then run the SAME attack again:
```bash
LAB_SECURE=1 python3 run_server.py
```
Re-run it: the secure app HTML-encodes the output, so you see `<script>` - inert text, not code.

Capture the flag on the CTF target, which has an XSS challenge where a simulated admin bot 'runs' your payload:
```bash
cd /workspaces/examto/ctf-lab
python3 -m venv .venv 2>/dev/null; . .venv/bin/activate; pip install -q -r requirements.txt
python3 target/run_target.py        # leave running
```

In a second terminal, send a `<script>` payload to `/greet`. The admin bot executes it and leaks its cookie in the `X-Admin-Cookie` response header:
```bash
curl -s -G -D - http://127.0.0.1:5000/greet --data-urlencode 'name=<script>alert(1)</script>' -o /dev/null | grep -i x-admin-cookie
```
The header value is the `FLAG{...}` - your capture answer.
hints: The payload is a <script> tag in the 'name' parameter.
Secure mode encodes < and > so the browser won't run it.
The capture is the 3-letter name of this flaw.

capture.task: **Capture the flag.** Land an XSS payload and submit the value of the `X-Admin-Cookie` header.
capture.hint: curl -D - with a <script> name, read X-Admin-Cookie
